terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Build the parts stock here and run it, after you call your functions from main.

tasks.title: Restock a part
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/stock.cpp`, write a function called `restock` that takes the stock as a reference to a `std::map<std::string, int>`, a part as a reference to a `const std::string` and a count as an `int`, and gives nothing back. It adds the count to that part in the caller's stock. A part that is not in the stock yet goes in with that count.

Check calls `restock` from code of its own with stocks of its own, an empty one included, and reads its stock after the call, so a function that changes a copy is found out.
nextSteps: Write the first line: the stock changes for the caller.
Add the count to the value under the part's name.
Think about a part that is not in the stock yet: what does `[]` do then?
In `main`, restock a part and print its count afterwards.
hints: The stock changes for the caller, so it is a reference without `const`.
`stock[part]` is the value under that key, and `[]` puts a missing key in with 0 first, so adding to it works for a new part too.
The shape is `void restock(std::map<std::string, int>& stock, const std::string& part, int count) { stock[part] += count; }`.

tasks.title: Look up a part without adding it
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, write a function called `countOf` that takes the stock as a reference to a `const std::map<std::string, int>` and a part as a reference to a `const std::string`. It gives back how many of that part are in the stock, as an `int`, or `0` when the part is not in it. Looking a part up leaves the stock as it was: no part is added.

Check calls `countOf` with stocks and parts of its own, parts that are not there included, and reads what it gives back and its stock afterwards.
nextSteps: Write the first line: two `const` references in, an `int` back.
Ask whether the part is in the stock, without `[]`.
When it is not, give back 0.
When it is, read its count with `.at()` and give it back.
hints: `[]` adds a key it does not find, so it is refused on a `const` map. Ask first.
`stock.count(part)` is 1 when the part is there and 0 when it is not. Once you know it is there, `stock.at(part)` reads its value without adding anything.
The shape is `if (stock.count(part) == 0) { return 0; } return stock.at(part);`.

tasks.title: Print the stock in order
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, write a function called `printStock` that takes the stock as a reference to a `const std::map<std::string, int>` and gives nothing back. It prints one line per part, in the map's own order, with the part's name, a colon, a space and the count. An empty stock prints the one line `Drawers empty`. Like this:

```
balance wheel: 2
crown: 3
```

Check calls `printStock` with stocks of its own, an empty one included, and reads what it prints. It only reads the stock, so the caller's stock must be the same afterwards.
nextSteps: Write the first line: a `const` reference to the map in, `void` back.
Go through the map with a range-based `for`.
Print each entry's key and value, and end each line.
hints: A range-based `for` goes through a map in the order of its keys, so there is nothing to sort.
Each entry is a pair: `.first` is the part's name and `.second` its count.
The shape is `for (const auto& entry : stock) { std::cout << entry.first << ": " << entry.second << "\n"; }`, after printing `Drawers empty` for an empty stock.

tasks.title: Count the parts used today
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 4`, write a function called `tally` that takes the parts used today as a reference to a `const std::vector<std::string>`, one name for each part used, and gives back a `std::map<std::string, int>` with each part's name and how many times it was used. A part that was not used is not in the map. With `{"crown", "mainspring", "crown"}`, the crown is in it twice and the mainspring once.

Check calls `tally` with lists of its own, an empty one included, and reads the map it gives back and its list afterwards.
nextSteps: Write the first line: a `const` vector in, a map back.
Make an empty map inside the function.
Go through the list, and count each part under its name.
Give the map back, and print it in `main` with your `printStock`.
hints: The map is new, made inside the function, and given back at the end, like the new vector in the last issue.
Here `[]` adding a missing key with 0 is just what is wanted: the first time a part is seen it starts at 0, and adding 1 makes it 1.
The shape is `std::map<std::string, int> counts; for (const auto& part : used) { counts[part]++; } return counts;`.
